edges.relationship: With Denise Henning (2021), Wheeler adopts Wolfe's definition: in the Americas 'classic colonialism evolved into settler colonialism', whose goal 'is the erasure of Indigenous peoples in order to establish settler rights to Indigenous lands and resources (Wolfe, 2006)'.
edges.evidence_note: Henning and Wheeler, New Directions for Student Services 2020, nos. 171–172 (online 30 April 2021), section 'Colonization and intergenerational trauma' (early-view p. 3; print pp. 57–67); Wolfe 2006 (Journal of Genocide Research 8:4) in the references. A co-authored study (Henning first author) of rural Indigenous students' postsecondary experience: it uses the frame as historical context and does not discuss settler colonial studies as a field. Her earlier colonial analysis used Blauner's colonial model (1998) and postcolonial and anti-colonial theory (2000, 2010), without settler-colonial vocabulary.

edges.relationship: Postcolonial studies as an internal challenge to conventional history that opens space for Indigenous history: Wheeler draws on Fanon and Memmi to name 'intellectual colonialism', the colonization of Indigenous histories (2000), and counts 'critical and post-/anti-colonial scholars' among her teachers (2010).
edges.evidence_note: Stevenson [Wheeler], Decolonizing Tribal Histories (PhD, UC Berkeley, 2000), p. 79 ('The imposition of eurocentric categories on Indigenous knowledge of the past amounts to intellectual colonialism'), p. 80 (Fanon quoted on colonialism's distortion of the past), pp. 117–118 (section 'Postcolonial Studies': Fanon and Memmi, with examples 'relevant to issues of Indigenous history … to demonstrate the value of postcolonial studies'); pages read through OCR. Wheeler 2010, p. 48.

edges.relationship: Native Studies does not belong under Ethnic Studies: to 'classify us as just another ethnic minority, it is colonialist'; 'we are not an ethnic minority … We are Indigenous', and 'Fourth World Studies is the next logical step' for comparison (1998; first given at UBC in 1995).
edges.evidence_note: Stevenson [Wheeler], Wicazo Sa Review 13:1 (1998): p. 33 (Native Studies 'does not belong under the rubric of Ethnic Studies'), p. 36 (Deloria's Custer Died for Your Sins on lumping minority groups together), pp. 34–38 (Blauner's colonial model, whose conclusion she accepts while criticising his evidence), p. 40 ('colonialist'), p. 49 (conclusion). First presented at UBC, 2 November 1995 (p. 50 note). Protocol passages (pp. 38–39) are not used (OCAP).

edges.relationship: Outside definitions misread Indigenous oral history: Vansina's process-and-product definition of oral tradition 'does not take into account that Indigenous Peoples' have their own respective intellectual histories' (1998); recorded oral histories are not documents, and treating transcripts as written records, as William Moss proposed, strips their cultural and linguistic context (2018).
edges.evidence_note: Stevenson [Wheeler], Saskatchewan History 50:2 (Fall 1998), p. 26 (re-read 2026-10-28 by OCR of the iPortal issue PDF). Wheeler, Shekon Neechie, 20 June 2018 (community-controlled: paraphrased, not reproduced): ¶1 (oral histories are not books and should not be treated as written records), ¶2 (against Moss's view of a taped interview as a document), ¶6 (what translation and transcription lose), ¶13 (scholars must learn to read recorded narratives in their own contexts). No Elder's words, teachings or story content are used (OCAP).

edges.relationship: Wheeler takes Smith's account of colonialism's negation of Indigenous views of history (2000) and her call for intellectual decolonization through Indigenous-framed research methods (2001).
edges.evidence_note: Stevenson [Wheeler], Decolonizing Tribal Histories (2000), p. 80 (block quotation of Smith 1999 on the 'negation of Indigenous views of history'; OCR). Wheeler, CJNS 21:1 (2001), p. 100: Smith 'and other like-minded Indigenous scholars promote anti-colonial research and argue for intellectual decolonization through the development of Indigenous-framed research methods and approaches (see Smith, 1999)'.

edges.relationship: Wheeler opens her case that Indigenous peoples are not an ethnic minority with Deloria's Custer Died for Your Sins (1969) on liberals who 'categorize them all together' as minority groups, and returns to him on cooperative movements (1998).
edges.evidence_note: Stevenson [Wheeler], Wicazo Sa Review 13:1 (1998), p. 36 (Deloria quoted, notes 6–9) and pp. 46–47 (Deloria 1969 on cooperative movements).

edges.relationship: Against the Supreme Court's 'mixedness' in Daniels (2016): '"mixed blood" does not equal Métis any more than "full blood" equals Indian. Both statements are based on racialized historical fictions'; the claim that the first Métis was born nine months after contact 'supports a colonial fantasy of benevolent relations'.
edges.evidence_note: Macdougall, International Indigenous Policy Journal 7:3 (2016), read in full: p. 2 (the Indian Act's 'legal fiction … that cannot now distinguish Indigenous cultural identities from colonial machinations'), p. 4 (the two quotations; the Métis as a nation formed in the fur trade, centred on kinship across a historic homeland), p. 5 (Métis and Non-Status Indians: 'we must be careful not to conflate national identities'). She cites Andersen 2016 (p. 1).

edges.relationship: Historians, McCallum argues, 'have created a false dichotomy between the colonial and modern period as two distinct projects'; for Indigenous women, 1940–80, colonialism continued as the state dictated schooling, employment and labour (2014, as summarised by Patricia Harms).
edges.evidence_note: Harms, review, Manitoba History 80 (Spring 2016), para. 2, read in full: 'Believing its destructive impact is in the past, historians, McCallum argues, have created a false dichotomy between the colonial and modern period as two distinct projects'; 'colonialism continued for Aboriginal women, as the state dictated education options, determined places of employment, and attempted to control women's labour practices'. Williams (BC Studies 191, 2016, read in full): her conclusion 'proposes a critical revision of historiographical methods and pedagogy in Indigenous and Canadian history'. McCallum's own text is unread; the edge rests on two named readers.

edges.relationship: In his article's abstract, challenges not the conclusion that upper Great Lakes fur-trade settlements were Métis but 'how they are ethnohistorically imagined as such', and appeals for a Métis 'counter-ethnohistory' anchored 'in an analytics of peoplehood' (2011, abstract)
edges.evidence_note: Abstract only, Andersen, Ethnohistory 58:1 (2011): the article examines how 'contemporary ethnohistorians examining upper Great Lakes fur trade settlements' handle 'the racialized logics governing the retrofitting of these settlements as “métis” and “Métis”' and 'the recent creep of juridical logics into ethnohistorical conversations'; 'Rather than challenging ethnohistorical conclusions that these settlements were/are Métis, this article challenges how they are ethnohistorically imagined as such'. His book (2014, p. 13, read) says chapter 2 explores 'the Powley decision's effects on government policy making and on upper Great Lakes ethnohistory'. The article body and chapter 2 are unread, and no ethnohistorian is named in the passages read, so the arrow goes to the field. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md)

edges.relationship: Finds 'the undertheorization of identity sitting at the heart of scholarship on the Canadian politics of recognition': Taylor's use of 'identity' conceals a tension between 'situated self-understanding' and 'official classification' (2014)
edges.evidence_note: Own words, 'Métis' (2014), introduction p. 14 (publisher sample, read), summarising chapter 5: two 'methodological shortcomings of Taylor's narrow use of identity': it 'marginalizes discussion of the extent to which the process of public recognition itself may prove constitutive to the claims of collective identity', and 'in positioning misrecognition as an external force, it overlooks how it also shapes the internal claims of the group'. Chapter 5 itself is unread. Distinct from Coulthard's critique of Taylor (edge_2132): Andersen keeps the concept of (mis)recognition (p. 20) and criticises Taylor's concept of identity. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md)

edges.relationship: Andersen uses (mis)recognition 'in keeping with my own Bourdieuvian tendencies': racialized categories 'rooted in colonial structures and practices, are seen and understood as natural' (2014)
edges.evidence_note: Own words, 'Métis' (2014), introduction p. 20 (publisher sample, read); the sample ends partway through his definition, which quotes Bourdieu. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md)

edges.relationship: Coulthard grounds his place-based critique in God Is Red: Deloria's 'distinction between Indigenous place-based and Western time-oriented understandings of the world' (2009)
edges.evidence_note: Coulthard's dissertation (2009), p. 88 (read): Deloria's 'groundbreaking 1972 text, God is Red' holds that Western societies derive meaning 'in historical/developmental terms, thereby placing time as the narrative of central importance'; the quoted distinction is Coulthard's own wording; p. 89: land as a field of 'relationships of things to each other' (quoting Deloria 2001). The passage that follows, on Dene relations to land, is community knowledge and is not used (OCAP). Whether the 2014 book keeps this reading is unchecked. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md)

edges.relationship: Coulthard reads Adams as the writer Fanon 'most influenced' and takes from him that Indigenous 'cultural self-empowerment can be captured or co-opted by the state apparatus and directed toward neo-colonial ends' (2009)
edges.evidence_note: Coulthard's dissertation (2009), pp. 188–194 (read): p. 188, Fanon 'most influenced the work of the late … historian and Red Power activist Howard Adams'; p. 193, 'There are a number of insights to be gleaned from Adams' engagement with the work of Fanon', first the co-optation quoted above, which he applies to the 1970s Dene movement; p. 194, Adams's call to revive traditions that empower and discard those that oppress, applied to Indigenous women's struggle against the Indian Act's patriarchal legacy. The biographical and autobiographical passages on pp. 188–190 are not used (OCAP). Whether the 2014 book keeps this reading is unchecked. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md)

edges.relationship: Coulthard takes from Canadian historians and geographers, citing Harris, that after the waves of settlement (1860–1914) colonial development 'required first and foremost land, and only secondarily' Indigenous labour: the historical ground of 'dispossession, not proletarianization' (2009)
edges.evidence_note: Coulthard's dissertation (2009), p. 18 (read): 'It is now generally acknowledged among Canadian historians and political economists' that Native labour became 'increasingly (although by no means entirely) superfluous'; n. 48 cites Harris, 'How Did Colonialism Dispossess?' (2004), p. 167, for the land-over-labour claim; n. 47 also cites Lutz, Makuk (2008), 'On the importance of Native labour'. Restated in the conclusion, p. 215: 'as most political economists and historians have now recognized'. A use, not a critique. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md)

edges.relationship: Native Canadians 'cannot enjoy fully "post-coloniality"'; a postcolonial reader that represents Natives 'only through non-Native Canadians' is 'unacceptable' (1999); the charge recurs in the 2010 book
edges.evidence_note: Own words, 1999 dissertation, PDF pp. 50–51 (read 2026-10-28): in The Post-Colonial Studies Reader 'no Native writers or scholars are included … I find it unacceptable in a postcolonial reader, especially one published in the 1990s, that Natives are represented only through non-Native Canadians'; 'Obviously, Native Canadians cannot enjoy fully "post-coloniality" since their colonial experience is imbricated with the past and present.' PDF p. 40: in Ashcroft, Griffiths and Tiffin 'it is the re/settler whites who are treated as the colonized resisting the mother country'. PDF p. 70: she will avoid the 'obscure language which has become such an uncontrollable part of post-colonial criticism'. 2010 book, p. 167, as quoted by Black (AICRJ 2011, p. 285, read in full): 'some scholars live in the illusion that … by their postcolonial powers of analysis, they have neutralized the colonial experience'. A critique of the field's scope and practice; she also uses its resources (Said, edge_2140). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md)

edges.relationship: Finds Sioui's call for 'an ethical approach to history' appealing but his autohistory 'at times obscure' on historical method, and his 'ideological portrait of Amerindians' too close to the Noble Savage (1999)
edges.evidence_note: Own words, 1999 dissertation, PDF pp. 240–241 (read 2026-10-28): 'Sioui's thesis on "autohistory" is at times obscure, especially when he turns to the issue of historical methodology'; it is 'not at all clear whether he is espousing a "division of labour" between white and Native (or Huron?) historians'; 'Parts of Sioui's proposal … is appealing, for example, his call for "an ethical approach to history"'; 'I have difficulty with his idealization … to the extent the portrait resembles the Noble Savage.' A qualified critique, distinct from her critique of Trigger's foreword to the same book (edge_2166). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md)

edges.relationship: Takes Fanon and Memmi as 'the classic sources' on internalised colonisation, while noting that The Wretched of the Earth does not treat Native North Americans (1999)
edges.evidence_note: Own words, 1999 dissertation (read 2026-10-28): PDF p. 48, 'Frantz Fanon and Albert Memmi are the classic sources for discussion on the processes of internalization'; PDF p. 12, classic (Fanon, Memmi) and contemporary works 'have convincingly shown that colonization produces a pervasive structural and psychological relationship between the colonizer and the colonized'; PDF p. 40 (qualification), 'Frantz Fanon in Wretched of the Earth does not deal with the treatment of Native North Americans either'. Parallel to edge_2140 (Said). Memmi has no node. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md)

edges.relationship: Reads Mandelbaum's The Plains Cree (1940) as dividing Cree technology 'into disparate pieces, giving the impression of a people frozen in time', a book taught without discussion of its 'Eurocentric assumptions' (1999)
edges.evidence_note: Own words, 1999 dissertation, PDF pp. 107–108 (read 2026-10-28), after Duchemin on Mackenzie's 'ethnographical curiosities': 'This is very similar to my reading of David Mandelbaum's treatment of Cree "tools" in The Plains Cree. Mandelbaum, one of the earlier anthropologists in the 1930s to study the Plains Cree, divides Cree technology into disparate pieces, giving the impression of a people frozen in time'; 'This book was first published in 1940 but I do not recall any discussion about its Eurocentric assumptions.' Her personal recollections on p. 108 are not used. Black (AICRJ 2011, p. 286) lists 'anthropologists (David Mandelbaum)' among the colonial authors treated in the 2010 book. Mandelbaum has no node. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md)

edges.relationship: Charges fur-trade historians with a 'double standard': Indians generalised as of 'covetous disposition' while European self-interest is overlooked; E. E. Rich 'persistently uses colonial phrases' such as 'crafty' and 'shrewd enough' (1999)
edges.evidence_note: Own words, 1999 dissertation (read 2026-10-28): PDF p. 102, 'It is quite common, for example, for fur trade historians to generalize Indians as having a "covetous disposition," quite obviously employing the double standard by over-looking European self-interests'; PDF p. 109, 'fur trade historian E.E. Rich persistently uses colonial phrases such as "crafty," "shrewd enough," "sophisticated enough" or "hardened enough" when describing Indians taking advantage of competition'; 'Even the more objective John C. Ewers qualifies his compliments'; she cites Walker (1971, p. 34) as noticing the same contradiction. The existing native_newcomer roster row already cites pp. 102, 109. Rich has no node or roster row; the strand holds the fur trade as national economic history. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md)

edges.relationship: Counts Dickason's The Myth of the Savage, by 'the prolific pace-setting scholar', among Native counter-works on the Indian image: 'clearly anti-colonial' (1999)
edges.evidence_note: Own words, 1999 dissertation (read 2026-10-28): PDF p. 190, works 'range from my slim Defeathering The Indian … to the voluminous The Myth of the Savage by the prolific pace-setting scholar Olive Patricia Dickason. Such productions have not been well understood as the resistance works that they in fact are'; PDF p. 191, the title 'represents more closely Western rather than Native tradition. Still, I consider it an expression of resistance for it is clearly anti-colonial.' PDF p. 21: she moves away from what Dickason calls 'that strain of tolerance toward Amerindians' in European thought, a qualified use. A reading and alignment, not a claim of personal debt. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md)

edge_2150.relationship: Decolonizing tribal histories: the 'silencing, marginalization, and patronizing of Indigenous voices' in the writing of Indigenous histories 'epitomizes intellectual colonialism', so decolonization 'must begin from within a tribal context' (2000); Native Studies is 'a revolt against colonialist representations of Indigenous life and history' (2001); oral history belongs 'in history, as history' (2010).

The board is carried by community_engaged_indigenous/indigenous_historians_institutions.

edge_2153.evidence_note: Paraphrased (Shekon Neechie, community-controlled: cited, not reproduced). 'Clearing the Plains of Accountability' (2018), para. 2 (his aim: to hold Daschuk's argument against the scholars he cites); paras. 5–8 (Tobias 1983, Lux 2004 and Titley 1999 set against Daschuk on Dewdney); para. 14 (whether those who praised the book read the foundational literature). 'Historians and Indigenous Genocide in Saskatchewan', para. 15 (Daschuk's attempt to exonerate Dewdney contradicts previous historians). Daschuk's words are known only through Innes. Revision 1.204 reroutes the edge from settler_colonialism/health_starvation to native_newcomer/reserves_schools_state. The critique concerns Daschuk's account of Dewdney and of the state-policy historians he cites (Tobias, Lux, Titley). Innes frames the deaths as 'colonial genocide' ('Historians and Indigenous Genocide', para. 1 and n. 1), not in settler-colonial terms; 'settler' appears only in his paraphrase of Daschuk ('Clearing the Plains of Accountability', paras. 3, 11).

edge_2164.relationship: Against 'the simplistic tropes of mixedness and hybridity that seem to fascinate so many scholars who write of Métis histories': asked 'Have not fur trade historians … already extensively documented numerous instances of Métis mixedness?', he answers that to understand the Métis 'in terms of some apparently innate mixedness is thus to reproduce the same racist depictions through which less critical commentators – among them scholars – recognize indigeneity' (2014)
edge_2164.evidence_note: His own words, 'Métis': Race, Recognition, and the Struggle for Indigenous Peoplehood (UBC Press, 2014), introduction read in the publisher's sample (pp. 3–14; pp. 3–20 rechecked 2026-10-28): p. 4, 'an overly racialized narrative that connected Métis nationhood to fur trade society'; p. 5, 'the simplistic tropes of mixedness and hybridity that seem to fascinate so many scholars who write of Métis histories', in 'a vision premised on the notion that all Indigenous peoples are mixed' (he does not deny mixedness); p. 10, 'Have not fur trade historians … already extensively documented numerous instances of Métis mixedness?'; p. 11, 'To continue to understand the Métis in terms of some apparently innate mixedness is thus to reproduce the same racist depictions'; p. 12, chapter 1 treats 'a strand of long-standing fur trade literature'. In the pages read he names no fur-trade historian, so the arrow targets the frame, not Van Kirk, Brown or Peterson. Their side in their own words: Peers and Podruchny (2010, n. 2) use 'metis' for 'all descendants of European men and Aboriginal women'; Brown, as translated there (pp. 2–3, n. 3): 'there is no single Metis core identity but rather a range along a spectrum'; Brown (2017, p. 57 n. 26) names The New Peoples and Andersen's book as the older and newer poles of the field and (pp. 57–58) offers 'of mixed descent' as a descriptive term beside 'the natives’ own categories'. Chapters 1–5 unread. Person entry, identity note and the book's source record are Agent B's. Bruce Trigger's foreword to George Sioui's For An American [sic] Autohistory provides a typical example of containment'; scholars 'must make it their mandate first to comprehend the noxious nature of colonization before dismissing utterances of decolonization merely as “sloganistic,” “bitter,” “biased” or “polemical”' (p. 136). edge_1003.evidence_note: Emma LaRocque's specified criticism in her 1999 University of Manitoba dissertation (read at PDF pp. 54 and 249); the arrow leaves from her entry since revision 1.204 (it left from the Indigenous history entry before her entry existed). She describes 'the neo cross-cultural approach adopted by Native specialist scholars from about the 1960s-1980s era (Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown, Van Kirk)', which 'tended to frame all things Native in typical terms of "cultural differences" or "traditions."' She grants: 'Compared to earlier racist material, this is, of course, a much improved approach to Native history. And with greater awareness, there is greater improvement.' But 'ethnological descriptions have a "distancing" effect', and 'This process results in Othering the very people the researcher is trying to make understandable to his or her audience' (p. 249). Her note 18 names the book: 'See in Many Tender Ties, for example, Van Kirk's listing of all the items of fashion or jewelry metis women were "very fond of" (101-103). There is an unstated assumption that such interests are abnormal or "remarkable" for these women to acquire' (p. 249, n. 18). In an earlier note she cites the book, with Saum and Ray and Freeman, among fur-trade studies that record Native resistance (PDF p. 54, note). Brown is named in the same list on p. 249 and the criticism is noted on her own entry (pe139_brown_rel_01); one arrow is drawn, to Van Kirk, because the note's example is hers. edge_868 (indigenous → native_newcomer) already carries LaRocque with Sioui and Stevenson (Wheeler) at entry level; this edge records the person-level target. OCR slips in the PDF text layer are corrected ('Van Krk', 'al1', 'hrterests'). The page numbers are PDF pages, as in edge_868. No identity classification is recorded. Later reading, labelled: Perry (2008, p. 163) dates 'sharp post-colonial, anti-racist, and post-structuralist critiques' of Van Kirk's work to the early 1990s; those texts are unread here.

Addendum 2026-10-14: Addendum 2026-10-14 (Claude, Van Kirk draft): reread at PDF p. 249 and n. 18 and at PDF p. 54 (OCR text layer; slips corrected). On p. 249 she describes 'the neo cross-cultural approach adopted by Native specialist scholars from about the 1960s-1980s era (Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown, Van Kirk)'. She grants that 'Compared to earlier racist material, this is, of course, a much improved approach to Native history', but writes that 'ethnological descriptions have a "distancing" effect' and that 'This process results in Othering the very people the researcher is trying to make understandable to his or her audience'. Note 18 cites Van Kirk's listing of fashion items metis women were 'very fond of' ('Many Tender Ties', pp. 101–103), with 'an unstated assumption that such interests are abnormal or "remarkable"'.
